input: Phase equilibrium for a binary mixture at fixed pressure is the state in which the two phases coexist without net transfer of either component between them. The equilibrium condition is equality of chemical potential across the phases: for each component, the chemical potential in one phase equals the chemical potential in the other. Net transfer stops at that equality because transfer is driven by a difference in chemical potential; a component moves from the phase in which its chemical potential is higher to the phase in which it is lower, and the movement continues until the difference is gone. Temperature is uniform across the phases in the same state, and the fixed pressure is common to both. Composition is where the two phases differ. Each phase has its own composition, and the equilibrium compositions are set by the chemical-potential equality, not by the overall composition of the mixture. The overall composition decides how much of each phase is present: a mixture rich in the more volatile component holds more of the phase in which that component concentrates. Changing the temperature at the fixed pressure shifts both equilibrium compositions, because the chemical potentials move with temperature and the equality is restored at new values. A mixture whose overall composition lies outside the range between the two equilibrium compositions exists as a single phase, since no pair of phases can satisfy the equality and the overall balance at once. The condition is stated here in words because it is the definition the rest of the subject uses: phase equilibrium is the equality of chemical potential for every component across every phase present, at uniform temperature and at the stated pressure.
